clinicalPearls: An autoimmune inflammatory orbitopathy most often associated with Graves disease, though patients may be hyperthyroid, euthyroid, or hypothyroid at presentation
Characteristic features include eyelid retraction, lid lag, proptosis (exophthalmos), and restrictive myopathy causing diplopia
The enlarged extraocular muscles typically spare their tendinous insertions on orbital imaging, a feature that helps distinguish it from orbital myositis
Disease runs an active inflammatory phase followed by a quiescent fibrotic phase, and treatment strategy depends on which phase and how severe the disease is
Smoking is a major modifiable risk factor that worsens severity and reduces treatment response
The sight-threatening complications are dysthyroid optic neuropathy from apical crowding and corneal exposure from severe proptosis and lid retraction

Management includes restoring and stabilising thyroid status, ocular surface lubrication, and, in active moderate-to-severe disease, immunosuppression with corticosteroids and, where appropriate, orbital radiotherapy
Orbital decompression relieves optic-nerve compression or disfiguring proptosis, with squint and lid surgery reserved for the stable phase
reference.pathophysiology: Thyroid eye disease is an autoimmune process in which autoantibodies, particularly against the thyrotropin receptor, activate orbital fibroblasts that share antigens with the thyroid gland. Activated fibroblasts proliferate, secrete glycosaminoglycans that draw water into the tissues, and can differentiate into fat cells, causing the extraocular muscles and orbital fat to swell within the bony orbit. This expansion produces proptosis, congestion, and restrictive myopathy, while the muscle bellies enlarge with relative sparing of their tendons. Crowding at the orbital apex can compress the optic nerve, and proptosis with lid retraction exposes the cornea. After the active inflammatory phase the enlarged muscles may fibrose, leaving fixed restriction and deformity.
additionalDifferentials: Orbital metastasis or IgG4-related orbital disease
additionalInvestigations: Thyroid function tests and thyroid autoantibodies including thyrotropin-receptor antibodies
Orbital CT or MRI showing fusiform muscle enlargement with tendon sparing
Assessment of visual acuity, colour vision, pupil reactions, and visual fields to detect optic neuropathy
Measurement of proptosis (exophthalmometry) and ocular motility with diplopia assessment
Corneal and ocular surface evaluation for exposure keratopathy
Disease activity and severity grading to guide treatment
redFlags: Reduced acuity, dyschromatopsia, or a relative afferent pupillary defect indicating dysthyroid optic neuropathy
Severe corneal exposure with breakdown from marked proptosis and lid retraction
Rapidly progressive proptosis or congestion in the active phase
Choroidal folds or disc swelling suggesting posterior compression
reference.prognosis: Many patients stabilise after the active phase with good outcomes, especially with smoking cessation and prompt treatment, but a minority develop sight-threatening optic neuropathy or corneal breakdown, and residual proptosis, lid malposition, and diplopia often require surgical rehabilitation in the stable phase.
pitfalls: Assuming normal thyroid function excludes the diagnosis, since patients can be euthyroid
Missing early dysthyroid optic neuropathy because proptosis and external signs may be modest
Not counselling about smoking as a key modifiable risk factor
Operating on lids or muscles before the disease has become inactive
Confusing tendon-sparing muscle enlargement with orbital myositis, which involves the tendons
management: Advise smoking cessation and restore stable euthyroidism, as smoking worsens severity and reduces treatment response

Treat active moderate-to-severe orbitopathy with immunosuppression, principally intravenous glucocorticoids, with orbital radiotherapy, rituximab or the IGF-1 receptor antibody teprotumumab as further options
Protect the ocular surface with lubricants and manage diplopia with prisms, considering selenium in mild disease
Grade disease activity and severity and monitor visual acuity, colour vision and pupillary responses to detect dysthyroid optic neuropathy
Treat sight-threatening optic neuropathy urgently with high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids and surgical orbital decompression when needed
Defer rehabilitative surgery until the disease is quiescent, performing orbital decompression, then strabismus, then eyelid surgery in sequence
Coordinate care in a joint ophthalmology-endocrinology clinic
